title: How To Break the Alzheimer’s Doom Loop
description: As a neuroscientist at high risk for Alzheimer’s disease, I’m constantly looking for new ways to protect my brain for the long haul. And a new paper that just dropped in Neuron had me smiling ear to ear because it reveals a previously unknown mechanism by which a well-known hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease drives the disease itself. Better yet, it points to solutions that I already have in my medicine cabinet. I’m going to break it down for you, starting with the science and then moving into practical tools you can start using today to help keep your brain sharp and healthy for decades to come. But first, some background. I want to introduce two key players: tau and mitochondria . Tau Tangles: A Hallmark of Alzheimer’s Disease You’ve probably heard of tau, particularly in the context of the neurofibrillary tangles seen in Alzheimer’s disease. In Alzheimer’s and certain other “tauopathies,” this protein, which normally sits on the cell’s cytoskeleton, becomes tagged with phosphate groups, a process known as “ hyperphosphorylation.” This causes tau to detach, clump together into aggregates called phospho-Tau neurofibrillary tangles , and contribute to neuronal dysfunction and death. This tau pathology is one of the major driving forces behind Alzheimer’s disease. Mitochondrial Dysfunction: Another Hallmark of Alzheimer’s Disease Now let’s talk about mitochondria, and then I’ll bridge the two. Mitochondria are, of course, “the powerhouse of the cell.” You’ve heard that before.

title: When Cholesterol Science Becomes Religion
description: If I take a step back and look at the state of cardiovascular medicine, I notice something conspicuous. We’ve invested decades of research and billions of dollars in the cholesterol hypothesis: the idea that high cholesterol—or, if we’re being more specific, LDL and ApoB-containing lipoprotein particles— causes cardiovascular disease. Therefore, the thinking goes, lowering these particles should reduce or even eliminate the disease. After all, if LDL is the central causal driver of atherosclerosis, then addressing them sufficiently should make the disease go away. That’s the simplistic narrative many of us are fed. And yet, we’ve been pursuing this model for half a century and have embarrassingly little to show for it. Cardiovascular disease remains the world’s leading killer. So, we should all be curious about what we obviously don’t understand. Right? However, I’ve also found that when you try to introduce nuance into this topic, it’s often treated not as valid scientific discourse, but as an ideological threat. Almost as if belief in the central importance of LDL cholesterol in cardiovascular disease is less a scientific model than a religion. And you don’t want to upset the priests. Let me begin to make my case with a short story, and then we’ll widen the lens to discuss a broader principle in medicine called the Overton Window, and why sometimes the moderate, reasonable point of view can look radical. A Cholesterol Question That Became Heresy Earlier this year, a paper was published in The New England Journal of Medicine —arguably the most influential medical journal in the world.

title: How to Lose Fat While Gaining Muscle (Proven by DEXA)
description: We used to think it was impossible to build muscle while losing fat—that you had to choose one or the other at any given point in time. I used to believe that myself. I was wrong. There’s nothing inherent in our biology that prevents us from doing both effectively at the same time. Let’s start with an example from our own StayCurious Metabolism community who, coincidentally, is actually named Nicholas N. Over the course of about a year and a half, he lost nearly half of his body fat, dropping almost 50 pounds of pure fat while gaining 25.6 pounds of muscle. No steroids or illicit compounds required.
